text: The Keeper's Ledgers
the far end of the highest shelf and found it
only half full. The last entry was dated 9
March of the present year, eleven days be-
fore he died. Wind south-west, force 5. Sea
moderate. Four vessels. The handwriting
had grown larger and less steady, but the
columns were as straight as ever.
Nora sat down on the bottom stair. She
had come intending to stay two nights, sign
whatever needed signing, and put the place
up for sale. She had a job to go back to, a
flat with a leaking tap, and a train booked
for Thursday at 2:15 p.m.
It was the harbormaster who explained
it, the following morning, over tea that was
nearly black. His name was Tom Garrity
and he had known Edmund for forty years.
"People think he was lonely out here," he
said. "He wasn't. He just liked things writ-
ten down. He said if nobody wrote it down,
it was as if the night hadn't happened."
"But who was it for?"
Garrity considered this. "There was a
trawler went missing in 1973," he said.
"The Marguerite, out of Peterhead. Six men
aboard. The inquiry wanted to know if
she'd passed the light, and when. Edmund
had it: twenty past one in the morning,
heading east, lights showing. It didn't save
anybody. But the families knew how far she
got." He put down his cup.
. "After that I
stopped asking who it was for."
She did not catch the Thursday train.
She told herself it was because of the
weather, which was true as far as it went:
the wind had gone round to the north and
the ferry was not running. She spent the
day carrying ledgers down to the kitchen
table, twelve at a time, and reading them in
order.
Most nights were dull. A few were not.
In February 1968 he had counted 43 ves-
sels sheltering in the lee of the island dur-
ing a storm that lasted three days. In
August 1979 he had written, without com-
ment, "Lights seen to the west at 02:10, low
on the water, not a ship." In the winter of
1985 there was a gap of a single night, and
beside it, in the margin, the words "In-
fluenza. Mrs. Garrity kept the count."
On Saturday the ferry ran again. Nora
walked down to the harbor, stood for some
time looking at the timetable, and then
walked back up the hill. That evening, a lit-
tle before dusk, she found a pencil, opened
the half-filled ledger to the first empty
page, and wrote the date at the top.
She did not know the proper way to de-
scribe the wind. She wrote "cold, from the
right." Then she pulled a chair to the win-
dow, and waited for the first ship.
